_doc: The Close constellation — the network of the material this piece is built from, and the four panels that read it. Sérgio, 2026-09-02: "I would still want to keep the idea of the Stars in the ceiling becoming the network of the data used to create this project with the 4 panels with the information." S101 keeps both halves: the stars over the seat open out into this network (src/room/pointCloud.ts), and each of the four eras gets ONE panel hanging over its own arc of anchors. ⚑ WHAT CHANGED IN THE SHAPE: every entry used to be a bare string on a golden-angle spread, so the mesh's topology said nothing. Each entry now carries the ERA OF THE PIECE IT GROUNDS — 0 for the project's own frame, which hangs overhead where the ceiling was, and 1-4 for the rooms — and the geometry follows it: one arc per era, at one bearing per era, so the player TURNS through 1997 → 2003 → 2016 → now, and the links run along each era and then across to the next. The cross-era links are the piece's own thesis and there are exactly three of them. ⚑ Era is the era each anchor GROUNDS IN THE PIECE, not the anchor's own date (Love Won Out ran from 1998; it grounds 2003's curricula). Cap: 32 (the label atlas's own row budget). No survivor names, no real individuals — sources and structures only. ⚑ Panel copy is Claude's draft under the 2026-08-17 norm; Sérgio owns dossier phrasing and every status, and his edit wins.

labels._doc: ⚑ S209 / P7-47 — the retro CD-ROM star: a press opens the Lexicon on Daniel's machine (app.ts)

⚑ S209i / ERA26-07 (his, 2026-10-03: 'one sourced sentence'). Was 'SEGM-Genspect-GETA mesh': 'mesh' asserted a link no source states (EVID-17), and nothing verified covers GETA here. Sentence verified in docs/research/E4_SOURCES_ai_2026-08-06.md (lines 31, 73), including their dispute of the listing.
labels.note: In June 2024 the Southern Poverty Law Center listed Genspect and SEGM (the Society for Evidence-Based Gender Medicine) as anti-LGBTQ hate groups. Both dispute the listing, saying it suppresses legitimate debate.

labels._doc: ⚑ S209j / ERA26-07 — from his Deep Research (~/Pc_Simulation/Sources/Deep Research/gate.md, 2026-10-03), recorded in VERIFY_CLOSE_LABELS_2026-10-03.md. Documented; the classification contested — both positions kept, unresolved. ⚑ Rewritten the same day (his: 'what is the point with this?'): the point is the WORD — the apparatus's 'exploring' (Lexicon e4 word of the day; 'identity exploration' in her related searches) and the rename to Therapy First, the Close message's 'when a practice is banned by name, it changes its name'.
labels.note: The word 2026 uses, “exploring”, has a source: a 2022 guide by the Gender Exploratory Therapy Association made “exploratory psychotherapy” the first step for young people with gender distress. Critics such as Florence Ashley say it works like a conversion practice under a gentler name; its authors deny it. The association has since renamed itself Therapy First.
labels.src: GETA, A Clinical Guide for Therapists Working with Gender-Questioning Youth (2022); Ashley, Perspectives on Psychological Science (2022); D'Angelo, Journal of Medical Ethics (2023)

labels._doc: ⚑ S209j / ERA26-07 — from his Deep Research (~/Pc_Simulation/Sources/Deep Research/gate.md, 2026-10-03), recorded in VERIFY_CLOSE_LABELS_2026-10-03.md. Was 'Genspect parent survey': the research found the 2025 instrument is an assessment questionnaire, not a published study (and a separate 2024 survey has no published methods) — so the label names the instrument and the sentence says what it is.
labels.note: Genspect's Parents' Survey is a questionnaire families fill in about their child and give to clinicians. It has not been published as a research study.
labels.src: Genspect, “The Genspect Parents' Survey: How It All Started” (2025)

labels._doc: ⚑ S209j / ERA26-07 — from his Deep Research (~/Pc_Simulation/Sources/Deep Research/gate.md, 2026-10-03), recorded in VERIFY_CLOSE_LABELS_2026-10-03.md. Was 'detransition cohort study (Fenway)': not a Fenway cohort but a secondary analysis of the 2015 U.S. Transgender Survey by authors at Stanford, the Fenway Institute, Harvard, BU and MGH. The sampling limit is kept in the sentence, as the research insists. ⚑ Rewritten the same day on his correction: pausing or stopping a transition is not questioning yourself — every respondent still identified as trans, and 'affirmation' was broadly defined (social steps included), so the study measures interruption by pressure, which is the very thing the 2026 apparatus counts as 'second thoughts'.
labels.note: Second Thoughts counts every stop as a change of mind. This study counted 2,242 trans and gender-diverse people who had paused or stopped a transition, social or medical, at some point: 82.5% named an outside pressure, such as family, stigma or safety. All of them still identified as trans. It measures transitions interrupted by pressure, not people who stopped being trans.
labels.src: Turban, Loo, Almazan and Keuroghlian, LGBT Health (2021); MacKinnon et al., Bulletin of Applied Transgender Studies (2022)

labels._doc: ⚑ S209i / ERA26-07 — verified in docs/research/E4_SOURCES_ai_2026-08-06.md line 73 (SPLC Hatewatch, 'Detransition narratives').
labels.note: The SPLC's Hatewatch reported how stories of detransition are used against trans people, and described detrans.ai as built on “reductive, anti-trans ideas and debunked pseudoscience”.

_panelsDoc: ⚑ S163 / R3-111: `status` is no longer stamped on the panel — it is shown in the frame (the menu's The Close's panels — sources), with `practices`: the dossier practices (data/dossier/practices.json keys) each panel's paragraph draws on, listed there with their sources. A press on a panel opens that list. ⚑ FOUR PANELS, ONE PER ERA, and they are the only prose in the Close. Rewritten 2026-09-12 (Sérgio: "think as someone who doesn't know the whole project, and needs a more clean and guided way to understand the content… too segmented"; and: "We don't have the proof to say that, we just are using information we found"). One flowing paragraph per era — who, what the machine did, why it matters — every general claim phrased as what the sources document, never as history; the last panel names itself speculative. `status` is the dossier law's own vocabulary (CLAUDE.md) and applies to the panel's claims as a whole. Each panel hangs beside its era's room plate (public/assets/close/era{N}.jpg, baked by tools/bake-close-plates.mjs) with the era's data cluster to its right. ⚑ They do NOT carry the title beat or `Restart as you are.` — those are the update's and the Restart card's. ⚑ S142: the 2016 panel said 'one day an item in her queue is about her' — the piece has no such item; its break is MALTA (s3_maiden.json), the law arriving in the group chat. Corrected to what the piece does.

panels.title: RECRUIT
panels.text: Daniel is sixteen. His mother has found a “family companion” programme on a message board and printed its questionnaire for him. It asks whether he has corrected the way he walks, talks and sits. Anonymous boards and mailing lists were used by conversion practices in their move online: a name for “the problem”, and a way out of it, offered to whoever searched.

panels.title: AUDIT
panels.text: Daniel is an adult, in the same room. The programme now lives on his computer as software. Every morning it asks how he is — Steady, Struggling, Grateful or Tired — and keeps the answer. It watches who he talks to; when a message arrives from someone outside, the programme sees it first. Peer accountability, and software that logged browsing and reported it to a partner, are documented; the streak and the machine that reads his messages are the piece's own compression of them. Here they carry the demand to change without anyone saying it out loud.

panels.title: GOVERN
panels.text: Vera works from her room, correcting other women’s writing for a platform — lesbian women, writing about their own lives — one rule at a time: remove anything unresolved, add the scripture. One afternoon the group chat on her phone is about a law: Malta has just made practices like hers an offence, unanimously. Nobody in the room says anything. Content rules and moderation work were among the tools these networks used to reach people at scale. In this room nobody is treated; the writing is edited.

panels.title: RESURGE
panels.text: Maya’s session is restored for her before she has touched anything. A companion finishes her search and suggests she wants to stop. Her record keeps her old name “for continuity of care”. Her photographs come back improved. A headset offers an immersive session. Then a friend’s invitation, inside that same headset, leads her somewhere the system cannot classify — a room where being trans is fine — and the update fails. This room is inferred. Around it, the record is not: in May 2026 the European Commission answered more than a million people asking for a ban on conversion practices with a non-binding recommendation, and declined to propose a law; organised campaigns against trans people’s care run across Europe. The room extends patterns that are already documented — autocomplete, retained records, photo enhancement, “support” agents — into a system that presents itself as care. What it cannot classify is other people.
